guidance: Requires professional medical monitoring. Focus on hydration with ORS and water. Avoid NSAIDs. Seek emergency care if warning signs appear: bleeding gums, persistent vomiting, severe belly pain, rapid breathing, blood in urine or stool.
precautions: Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen — use only paracetamol

guidance: Consult a doctor immediately for rapid diagnostic test (RDT) and antimalarial prescription. Recovery requires completing the full drug course (usually Artemisinin-based combination). Keep hydrated and rest. Falciparum malaria requires hospitalization.
precautions: Strict compliance with prescribed medication — stopping early causes drug resistance
Prevent mosquito bites using repellents, nets, and full clothing
Drain stagnant water near your home

guidance: Consult a healthcare provider for antibiotic prescription (azithromycin or ceftriaxone). Drink only boiled or purified water. Eat plain, easy-to-digest cooked meals. Strict hand hygiene is critical.
precautions: Wash hands before eating and after using washroom
Avoid raw foods and street food during illness
Drink only boiled or bottled water
Typhoid Vi vaccine provides good protection

guidance: TB is curable with a full 6-month DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment Short-course) medication course under RNTCP/NikshayMitra program (free in India). Never stop treatment early even if feeling better — it causes drug-resistant TB. Isolate while infectious (first 2 weeks of treatment).
precautions: Cover mouth with tissue or elbow when coughing
Ensure good ventilation in living areas
All household contacts should be screened
HIV-positive individuals are at very high risk and need regular screening

guidance: No specific antiviral treatment. Rest and supportive care. Maintain nutrition and hydration. Avoid alcohol completely. Most recover fully in a few weeks. Hospitalization for severe cases.
precautions: Wash hands thoroughly especially after toilet use and before eating

guidance: Acute Hepatitis B: supportive care. Chronic Hepatitis B: requires long-term antiviral therapy (tenofovir, entecavir). Regular liver function tests and monitoring are essential. Avoid alcohol. Vaccination available and recommended for all.
precautions: Do not share needles, razors, or toothbrushes
All newborns should receive Hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth

symptoms: sudden onset profuse watery diarrhea (rice-water stool)
guidance: EMERGENCY — Immediate rehydration with ORS or IV fluids is life-saving. Start ORS immediately: 1 packet in 1 liter boiled water. Antibiotics (doxycycline) shorten duration. Seek hospital care immediately. Can be fatal within hours if untreated.
precautions: Drink only treated or boiled water
Eat only cooked and hot food
Oral cholera vaccine available in outbreak settings

symptoms: severe joint pain (especially hands, wrists, ankles, feet)
joint pain may persist for months
guidance: No specific antiviral. Rest, hydration, and pain management with paracetamol. Avoid NSAIDs during fever phase. Joint pain may be prolonged — physiotherapy helps. Warm compresses on affected joints for relief.
precautions: Mosquito prevention: repellents, long sleeves, bed nets
Eliminate water containers where mosquitoes breed
Joint pain can last weeks to months — follow up with doctor

guidance: Mild cases: rest at home, monitor oxygen with pulse oximeter, stay hydrated. Isolate for at least 5 days. Seek emergency care if SpO2 drops below 94%, severe breathlessness, persistent chest pain, or confusion. Vaccination significantly reduces severe disease.
precautions: Wear mask in crowded or enclosed places
Isolate if positive to protect vulnerable family members

symptoms: excessive salivation — symptoms appear weeks to months after bite
guidance: EMERGENCY AFTER ANIMAL BITE: Immediately wash wound thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes. Go to hospital NOW for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) — vaccine + immunoglobulin. PEP is nearly 100% effective if given before symptoms. Once symptoms appear, rabies is almost always fatal.
precautions: Wash animal bite wound immediately with soap and water
Report to nearest PHC/hospital within hours of any dog/bat/monkey bite
Do not handle wild or stray animals

symptoms: in severe cases: liver failure, kidney failure, bleeding
guidance: Seek medical care immediately. Antibiotics (doxycycline or penicillin) are effective early in the disease. Severe cases need hospitalization. Common after floods — avoid wading in floodwater.
precautions: Avoid wading in floodwater or soil contaminated by rodent urine
Wear rubber boots and gloves when working in soil or water
Doxycycline prophylaxis can be used for high-risk exposures

symptoms: many infections are mild or asymptomatic
guidance: No specific antiviral treatment. Intensive supportive care in hospital for severe cases. Vaccination is the most effective prevention. Common in rural rice-growing areas near pig farms and water bodies.
precautions: Vaccination recommended for residents and travelers in endemic areas
Use mosquito repellents and bed nets
Avoid outdoor activity at dusk and dawn when mosquitoes are most active

symptoms: pale or reddish patches on skin with loss of sensation
numbness in hands, feet, or face
painless wounds on hands and feet
guidance: Leprosy is curable. Free Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) is available at all PHCs in India under the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP). Treatment lasts 6-12 months. Early treatment prevents permanent disability. Leprosy has very low transmission.
precautions: Early detection and treatment is key to preventing disability
MDT is available free at all government health facilities
Treat skin patches early — do not ignore numbness
Regular follow-up with health worker during treatment

symptoms: prolonged irregular fever lasting weeks to months
guidance: Seek medical care immediately. Kala-azar is treated with antileishmanial drugs (liposomal amphotericin B — available free under NVBDCP program). Untreated Kala-azar is almost always fatal. India aims to eliminate Kala-azar.
precautions: Use sandfly nets (fine-mesh) as sandflies that transmit disease are tiny
Apply insecticide to walls of homes
Early reporting of fever cases to ASHA workers

symptoms: swelling of legs, arms, or genitals (lymphedema)
recurring fever with swollen lymph nodes
many infections are asymptomatic for years
guidance: Annual Mass Drug Administration (MDA) of Albendazole + DEC tablets is available free under the National Filaria Control Programme. Lymphedema management: keep limbs clean, do exercises, elevate limbs while sleeping. Surgery for hydrocele.
precautions: Participate in annual MDA drives in your district
Prevent mosquito bites using repellents and nets
Maintain good hygiene of affected limbs to prevent secondary infections
Report swelling of limbs to ASHA worker or PHC

symptoms: burrow tracks on skin (thin zigzag lines)
rash in skin folds (between fingers, wrists, elbows, armpits, waist, genitals)
guidance: Apply permethrin 5% cream from neck down, leave overnight, wash off next day. Treat all household members simultaneously even if asymptomatic. Wash all clothing and bedding in hot water on same day.
precautions: Treat all household contacts at the same time
Wash all clothes, bedding, and towels in hot water
Do not share clothing or bedding
Avoid close physical contact with infected persons

symptoms: circular ring-shaped red rash with clear center
hair loss in affected area (scalp ringworm)
guidance: Apply antifungal cream (clotrimazole, terbinafine) twice daily for 2-4 weeks. Keep area clean and dry. Do not stop treatment when rash disappears. Severe or widespread cases need oral antifungals from a doctor.
precautions: Keep skin dry especially skin folds and between toes
Do not share combs, towels, or clothing
Wear flip-flops in public showers and pools
Treat pets if they have ringworm

symptoms: early: flu-like symptoms, fever, swollen lymph nodes, rash, sore throat
later: weight loss, chronic diarrhea, night sweats, recurrent infections, oral thrush, prolonged fatigue
guidance: HIV is manageable with lifelong Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) — available FREE at all ART centers in India under NACO. Early treatment allows near-normal lifespan. Test regularly if at risk. ART also prevents transmission to partners and children.
precautions: Do not share needles or syringes
HIV-positive pregnant women must take ART to prevent transmission to baby
Get tested — knowing your status protects you and others

symptoms: rash that does not fade when pressed (in bacterial meningitis)
guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Go to hospital immediately. Bacterial meningitis is life-threatening and requires IV antibiotics urgently. Every hour of delay increases risk of death or permanent disability (deafness, brain damage). Do not wait.
precautions: Avoid close contact with infected person
Seek emergency care for severe headache with stiff neck and fever

symptoms: gray or white membrane on throat or tonsils
guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Requires immediate hospitalization and antitoxin plus antibiotics (penicillin or erythromycin). The membrane can block airways leading to suffocation. DPT/Td vaccination is the most effective prevention.
precautions: Ensure full DPT vaccination for children
Td booster every 10 years for adults
All contacts should receive antibiotics prophylactically

symptoms: stiffness of neck, shoulders, and back
muscle spasms triggered by sound or touch
guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Requires immediate hospitalization, tetanus antitoxin (TIG), antibiotics, and wound care. Even with treatment, tetanus has high mortality. Prevention through vaccination is critical. Wound care after injury is essential.
precautions: Ensure TT (Tetanus Toxoid) vaccination is up to date — booster every 10 years
Clean all wounds immediately with soap and water
Seek medical care for all puncture wounds, animal bites, or dirty wounds
Pregnant women must receive TT vaccine

symptoms: mild cough progressing to severe coughing fits
characteristic whooping sound after cough in children
infants may turn blue (cyanosis) during fits
guidance: Antibiotics (azithromycin) if started early reduce infectiousness. Supportive care for coughing fits. Small, frequent meals to reduce vomiting. Infants are at highest risk of severe disease and complications (pneumonia, brain damage). Hospitalize infants.
precautions: Ensure DPT/Tdap vaccination for children and Tdap booster for pregnant women
Isolate infected person for 5 days after starting antibiotics
Caregivers of infants should be vaccinated (cocooning strategy)
Seek immediate care for any infant with severe cough

guidance: Rest, hydration, and symptomatic relief with paracetamol. Antiviral (oseltamivir) can reduce duration if started within 48 hours. High-risk groups (elderly, pregnant, chronic illness) need prompt medical care. Annual flu vaccine is best prevention.
precautions: Stay home when sick to avoid spreading

symptoms: chest pain that worsens with breathing
guidance: Bacterial pneumonia requires antibiotics (prescribed by doctor). Viral pneumonia requires supportive care. Hospitalization for severe cases. Pneumococcal and flu vaccines prevent many cases. Watch for difficulty breathing — seek emergency care.
precautions: Pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13, PPSV23) for children and elderly
Seek care for persistent cough with fever

symptoms: red blotchy skin rash starting on face and spreading down
guidance: Supportive care — rest, hydration, fever management. Vitamin A supplementation reduces complications. Serious complications include pneumonia and encephalitis. Unvaccinated children are at highest risk. Measles is highly contagious — isolate.
precautions: Ensure full MMR vaccination for children (2 doses)
Isolate infected person for 4 days after rash appears
Seek care if breathing difficulty or confusion develops

symptoms: swollen painful salivary glands (one or both sides)
guidance: Supportive care — rest, hydration, pain relief (paracetamol). Apply warm or cold compresses to swollen glands. Avoid acidic foods that stimulate saliva. Rare complications: orchitis (testicle swelling), meningitis, deafness. MMR vaccine prevents.
precautions: Isolate for 5 days after swelling begins

symptoms: red rash starting on face and spreading to body
guidance: Mild illness — supportive care. Main danger is to pregnant women: can cause congenital rubella syndrome in fetus (deafness, heart defects, cataracts). Rubella vaccination (MMR) is critical for women of childbearing age.
precautions: Pregnant women should avoid contact with infected persons
Blood test for rubella immunity before pregnancy
Isolate for 7 days after rash appears

symptoms: itchy blister-like rash starting on face, chest, back
rash progresses from red spots to fluid-filled blisters to scabs
guidance: Supportive care — calamine lotion for itching, oatmeal baths, paracetamol for fever. Avoid scratching to prevent bacterial infection. Aspirin not to be given to children (Reye's syndrome risk). Antiviral (acyclovir) for high-risk cases. Highly contagious.
precautions: Isolate until all blisters have crusted over (usually 5-7 days)
Do not scratch to avoid scars and infection
Pregnant women and immunocompromised need prompt care

symptoms: mild: fever, fatigue, headache, vomiting, neck stiffness
severe: sudden flaccid paralysis in arms or legs
guidance: No cure for polio — treatment focuses on supportive care, physical therapy, and rehabilitation. Prevention through vaccination is the only solution. Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) and Injectable Polio Vaccine (IPV) are used globally in eradication efforts.
precautions: Ensure full polio vaccination as per schedule (OPV/IPV)
Report any case of sudden flaccid paralysis to health authorities
Booster doses for travelers to endemic areas

guidance: No specific treatment — rest, hydration, paracetamol for fever. Main danger is to pregnant women: Zika causes microcephaly and other severe birth defects. Pregnant women must avoid travel to endemic areas and prevent mosquito bites.
precautions: Pregnant women should avoid endemic areas
Practice safe sex to prevent sexual transmission

symptoms: after a brief remission: jaundice, bleeding, kidney failure, abdominal pain (toxic phase)
guidance: Supportive care in hospital for severe cases. No specific antiviral. Yellow fever can be fatal (20-50% of severe cases). Prevention through vaccination is highly effective and mandatory for travel to endemic areas. Avoid mosquito bites.
precautions: Yellow fever vaccination (single dose provides lifelong protection)
Avoid travel to endemic areas without vaccination
Report to health authorities — yellow fever is notifiable

guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Requires immediate isolation and intensive supportive care. Ebola has high mortality. No specific cure — experimental treatments (monoclonal antibodies) are used. Strict infection control is essential. Contact tracing crucial.
precautions: Health workers must wear full PPE
Avoid contact with blood and bodily fluids

symptoms: in severe cases: meningitis, encephalitis, paralysis
guidance: No specific antiviral. Supportive care. Severe cases require hospitalization. Transmission via mosquito bites. Most infections are asymptomatic.
precautions: Mosquito prevention: repellents, long sleeves, nets
Avoid outdoor activity at dusk and dawn

symptoms: in severe cases: eye damage, encephalitis, hemorrhagic fever, liver failure
guidance: No specific treatment. Supportive care. Most cases are mild. Severe cases require hospitalization. Transmission via mosquito bites or contact with infected animal blood/fluids. Common in livestock areas.
precautions: Wear gloves when handling animal blood or tissues

symptoms: bleeding from gums, nose, or other sites in severe cases
guidance: Immediate medical care. Supportive care with fluids and electrolytes. Antiviral (ribavirin) effective if started early. Transmission via contact with rat urine, feces, or contaminated food. Health worker infection risk.
precautions: Avoid contact with rats — store food in sealed containers

guidance: EMERGENCY — Requires immediate isolation and intensive supportive care. No specific antiviral. High fatality rate. Strict infection control. Contact tracing crucial.
precautions: Avoid contact with bats and primates in endemic areas

guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Isolation and intensive supportive care. No specific antiviral. Transmission via contact with fruit bats, contaminated fruit (date palm sap), or infected person's bodily fluids. Health worker precautions critical.
precautions: Avoid eating fruits with bite marks from bats
Avoid drinking raw date palm sap

guidance: Treat with antibiotics (azithromycin or doxycycline) — partner must also be treated. Untreated chlamydia causes infertility and PID in women. Test if you have a new or multiple sexual partners. Follow-up test 3 months after treatment.
precautions: Both partners must be treated simultaneously

guidance: Treat with dual antibiotic therapy (ceftriaxone + azithromycin) — resistance is growing. Partner treatment is essential. Untreated can cause PID, infertility, and disseminated infection. Test if at risk. Retesting 3 months after treatment.
precautions: Partner notification and treatment is essential
Antibiotic resistance is increasing — get tested and treated properly
All pregnant women should be screened

symptoms: PRIMARY: painless sore (chancre) at site of infection — heals in weeks
SECONDARY: rash on palms and soles, fever, swollen lymph nodes, hair loss, mouth sores
TERTIARY: neurological, cardiovascular, or organ damage years later
guidance: Treat with penicillin — highly effective. Partner treatment essential. Can be transmitted to fetus (congenital syphilis) leading to stillbirth, deafness, and neurological damage. Screen all pregnant women. Follow-up antibody tests needed to monitor response.
precautions: Take penicillin as prescribed — no alternatives for pregnant women

symptoms: most infections are asymptomatic and clear naturally
usually no symptoms until precancer or cancer develops
guidance: HPV is the most common STI and is cleared by the immune system in most women. High-risk types (16, 18) cause cervical cancer. HPV vaccine available free under government program for girls age 9-14. Pap smear/VIA screening every 3-5 years for women 30-65.
precautions: HPV vaccine for girls 9-14 (free under government program)
Use condoms (reduce but do not eliminate risk)
Do not smoke — increases cervical cancer risk in HPV-positive women

symptoms: painful blisters/sores in genital or anal area
tingling or itching before sores appear
guidance: Antiviral medications (acyclovir, valacyclovir) reduce outbreak severity and frequency. They do not cure but suppress the virus. Avoid sexual contact during outbreaks. Use condoms to reduce transmission. Inform partners.
precautions: Take daily suppressive antivirals if frequent outbreaks
Do not share towels during outbreaks
Pregnant women: inform doctor — may need medication at delivery

symptoms: green-yellow vaginal discharge with fishy odor
guidance: Treat with single-dose oral antibiotic (metronidazole or tinidazole). Partners must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection. Avoid alcohol during treatment (severe reaction). It increases HIV acquisition risk.
precautions: Both partners must be treated at the same time
Recurrence is common if partners not treated

symptoms: no bad odor (distinguishes from bacterial vaginosis)
guidance: Antifungal cream or suppository (clotrimazole, miconazole) for 1-7 days. Oral fluconazole single dose. Avoid tight synthetic underwear. Do not douche. Recurrent infections need medical evaluation for underlying conditions (diabetes, immunosuppression).
precautions: Do not douche — disrupts normal flora
Treat sexual partners only if recurrent — not routine
See doctor if infection recurs within 2 months

symptoms: thin gray-white discharge with a strong fishy odor (worse after sex)
guidance: Treat with antibiotics (metronidazole or clindamycin) — oral or vaginal. Partners do not need routine treatment. BV increases risk of STIs and preterm birth if pregnant. Recurrence is common.
precautions: Do not use scented soaps or bubble baths
Pregnant women: treatment reduces preterm birth risk

guidance: Antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, azithromycin) based on susceptibility. ORS for hydration. Handwashing is critical — highly contagious. Do not use anti-diarrheal drugs (loperamide) — they worsen infection.
precautions: Do not prepare food for others while ill

guidance: Usually self-limiting — hydration is key. Antibiotics (azithromycin) for severe cases or immunocompromised. Common from undercooked poultry and unpasteurized milk. It can trigger Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Treat with antiparasitic drugs (metronidazole, tinidazole). Avoid alcohol during treatment. Good hand hygiene prevents spread. Source: contaminated water, daycares, oral-anal sex.
precautions: Wash hands after toilet and before food
Do not swim if having diarrhea
Treat all household members if outbreak

symptoms: mild diarrhea to severe dysentery (bloody stools)
liver abscess in extraintestinal form — fever, right upper quadrant pain
guidance: Treat with metronidazole (luminal agent plus tissue agent). Intestinal infection plus liver abscess need different drug combinations. Source: contaminated food/water, especially in tropical areas.
precautions: Do not ignore liver pain with fever — seek care
Screening for asymptomatic carriers in food handlers

symptoms: passage of live worms in stool
guidance: Treat with single-dose albendazole or mebendazole. Deworming programs in India (National Deworming Day) for children and pregnant women. Reinfection is common in poor sanitation areas.
precautions: Children should be dewormed every 6 months
Wash hands after playing in soil

symptoms: itching at site of skin penetration
iron deficiency anemia (blood loss from gut)
guidance: Albendazole is effective. Iron supplements for anemia. Prevent by wearing shoes. Common in rural areas with poor sanitation. Anemia in women of reproductive age is a major consequence.
precautions: Sanitation: prevent fecal contamination of soil
Regular deworming for children and at-risk groups
Treat anemia with iron and folic acid

symptoms: in children: growth retardation, rectal prolapse (heavy infection)
guidance: Albendazole or mebendazole for 3 days. Severe infections need prolonged treatment. Associated with poverty and poor sanitation.

symptoms: intense perianal itching, especially at night
visible tiny white worms in stool or perianal area
guidance: Two doses of mebendazole or albendazole 2 weeks apart. Treat entire household. Hygiene: washing hands, changing underwear daily, showering in morning to remove eggs. Eggs survive on surfaces for 2-3 weeks.
precautions: Change underwear daily and wash in hot water
Bathe in the morning to remove eggs from skin

symptoms: skin rash (larva currens — moving rash on buttocks and thighs)
guidance: Ivermectin is the treatment. Do not use steroids without treating — causes hyperinfection. Strongyloides can persist for decades. Screen in immunocompromised patients from endemic areas.
precautions: Avoid walking barefoot in endemic areas
If immunocompromised, get tested for Strongyloides
Do not use corticosteroids without antihelminthic if at risk

guidance: Antibiotics (azithromycin, ceftriaxone) based on culture sensitivity. Same precautions as typhoid. Good hand hygiene. Water and food safety.
precautions: Same as typhoid: safe water, cooked food, handwashing
Vaccination (no specific paratyphoid vaccine — typhoid vaccine offers partial protection)

guidance: Requires prolonged combination antibiotics (doxycycline + rifampicin) for 6 weeks. Relapse risk. Source: unpasteurized dairy products, contact with infected animals (farmers, butchers).
precautions: Wear gloves when handling animal tissues

guidance: Doxycycline for acute infection. Endocarditis requires prolonged treatment. Source: inhalation of aerosols from infected animals (sheep, goats, cattle). Common in animal workers.
precautions: Wear masks when handling animal products

symptoms: rash (starts on wrists and ankles spreading centrally)
eschar (black crust) at tick bite site
guidance: Doxycycline is effective and should be started empirically without waiting for lab results. Tick-borne diseases are increasing in India. Avoid tick bites.
precautions: Wear long sleeves in tick areas
Check for ticks after outdoor activities

symptoms: eschar at mite bite site (often hidden)
guidance: Doxycycline or azithromycin. High index of suspicion needed — eschar may be hidden in skin folds. Common in rural areas. If untreated, mortality is high. Free treatment at PHCs in endemic areas.
precautions: Wear long clothing in grassy areas

symptoms: BUBONIC: swollen painful lymph nodes (buboes), fever, chills, weakness
SEPTICEMIC: fever, abdominal pain, shock, bleeding
PNEUMONIC: severe cough, bloody sputum, chest pain, highly contagious airborne
guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Immediate isolation and antibiotics (streptomycin, gentamicin, doxycycline). Pneumonic plague requires respiratory isolation. Notifiable disease. Infected rat fleas transmit.
precautions: Pneumonic plague patients require airborne precautions

symptoms: CUTANEOUS: painless skin sore turning into black eschar, with edema
PULMONARY: severe flu-like, pneumonia, hemorrhagic mediastinitis (high mortality)
GASTROINTESTINAL: nausea, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea
guidance: Antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, doxycycline). Cutaneous is treatable, pulmonary is often fatal despite treatment. Source: contact with infected animals or animal products. Vaccine for high-risk occupations.
precautions: Wear protective gear handling animal products

symptoms: skin sores that start as papules and develop into ulcers with raised edges
can take weeks to months to develop
endemic in parts of India (Rajasthan, Bihar)
guidance: Treatment based on species and severity — local heat therapy, intralesional drugs, or systemic antimony/amphotericin. Not usually life-threatening but causes disfiguring scars.
precautions: Eliminate sandfly breeding sites (cracks in walls, damp areas)

symptoms: destructive lesions in nose, mouth, and throat
ulceration leading to disfigurement (destroys nasal septum, lips)
guidance: Systemic antimony or amphotericin B. Can be difficult to treat. Refer to specialist. Causes severe disfigurement if untreated. Endemic in South America, rare in India.
precautions: Early treatment of cutaneous lesions prevents mucosal spread
Do not ignore nasal symptoms in endemic areas

symptoms: early: fever, headache, joint pain, lymphadenopathy
later: confusion, sleep disturbances, personality changes, difficulty walking, coma (meningoencephalitis)
guidance: Diagnosis requires CSF examination for stage. Treatment: pentamidine (early) or melarsoprol/eflornithine (late CNS). Medical emergency. Endemic in sub-Saharan Africa. Tsetse fly bite transmits.
precautions: Avoid tsetse fly bites (repellents, neutral-colored clothing)
Wear long sleeves in savannah areas
Screen travelers returning from endemic areas

symptoms: ACUTE: fever, fatigue, swelling at bite site (Romaña's sign: eyelid swelling)
CHRONIC: cardiomyopathy (arrhythmias, heart failure), megaesophagus, megacolon, decades after infection
guidance: Benznidazole or nifurtimox in acute and early chronic. No effective treatment for advanced cardiac/GI complications. Transmitted by kissing bugs (reduviid) in the Americas. Also blood transfusion.
precautions: Prevent bug bites with repellents and bed nets
Pregnant women at risk should be screened

symptoms: chronic: blood in urine (S. haematobium → bladder cancer), abdominal pain, diarrhea, liver fibrosis (S. mansoni), neurological complications
guidance: Praziquantel is highly effective. Avoid freshwater swimming in endemic areas (Africa, Middle East). Snails are intermediate hosts. Mass drug administration in endemic areas.
precautions: Avoid swimming in freshwater in endemic areas
Treat infected individuals in endemic communities

symptoms: if cysts die — inflammation, edema, increased intracranial pressure
guidance: Antiepileptic drugs for seizures. Albendazole/praziquantel with steroids to manage inflammation. Avoid pork tapeworm infection by cooking pork thoroughly. Prevent fecal-oral spread.
precautions: Sanitation to prevent fecal contamination of pig feed

symptoms: passing segments (proglottids) in stool or clothing
guidance: Praziquantel or niclosamide single dose. Cook beef (T. saginata) and pork (T. solium) thoroughly. Handwashing. Prevent contamination of food with human feces.
precautions: Cook meat to safe internal temperature
Freeze meat for 12 days to kill cysts
Do not eat raw or undercooked meat

symptoms: liver: RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, obstructive jaundice
guidance: Surgical removal (excision) or PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, reaspiration). Albendazole pre- and post-surgery. Prevent via hygiene around dogs (source of eggs).
precautions: Do not feed dogs raw offal
Community health education in pastoral areas

symptoms: vitamin B12 deficiency → megaloblastic anemia (due to worm consuming B12)
guidance: Praziquantel single dose. Cooking fish thoroughly kills larvae. Freezing at -20°C for 7 days also kills. Raw fish (sushi) is a source.
precautions: Freeze fish for 7 days if eating raw

symptoms: in immunocompromised: encephalitis, confusion, seizures, focal deficits
congenital: hearing loss, intellectual disability, blindness, hydrocephalus
guidance: Healthy: self-limiting. Immunocompromised: treat with sulfadiazine + pyrimethamine + leucovorin. Pregnant women: spiramycin to prevent fetal transmission. Avoid cat feces and raw/undercooked meat.
precautions: Pregnant women: avoid changing cat litter
Do not consume unpasteurized goat milk

symptoms: eye involvement: vision loss, retinal granuloma
guidance: Albendazole or mebendazole. Steroids for eye inflammation. Prevent by deworming pets, handwashing after soil contact. Children are at highest risk.
precautions: Wash hands after playing in soil
Cover sandboxes when not in use
Do not let dogs defecate in children's play areas

symptoms: same as leptospirosis but with jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhage, pulmonary hemorrhage, myocarditis
guidance: EMERGENCY — IV penicillin, doxycycline. Supportive care for organ failure. Common after floods. Dialysis may be needed. Prevention is key.
Doxycycline or azithromycin. Notify public health. Avoid contact with sick birds. Wear masks when cleaning bird cages.
precautions: Wear masks and gloves when cleaning bird cages
Practice hand hygiene after bird contact

symptoms: source: contaminated water systems (AC cooling towers, humidifiers, showers)
guidance: Antibiotics (azithromycin, levofloxacin). Hospitalization for severe. Outbreak investigation. Maintain water systems to prevent Legionella growth.
precautions: Regular maintenance of AC cooling towers

guidance: Treat with IV ceftazidime or carbapenem for 2 weeks, followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 3-6 months. Source: soil and water in endemic areas (SE Asia, India).
precautions: Avoid contact with soil and water if immunocompromised
Wear boots and gloves in endemic areas

symptoms: ulceroglandular: skin ulcer + swollen lymph nodes
typhoidal: fever, septicemia without local lesion
guidance: Streptomycin or gentamicin. Doxycycline or ciprofloxacin as alternatives. Source: handling infected animals (rabbits, rodents), tick bites, or contaminated water.
precautions: Wear gloves when handling wild animals
Avoid drinking untreated water in endemic areas

guidance: Doxycycline early in course. ORS. If no improvement in 48 hours, needs hospitalization. Prevention: avoid floodwater, rodent control.

symptoms: LATE: arthritis (knee), neurological (Bell's palsy, meningitis), cardiac (AV block)
guidance: Doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime for 14-21 days. Early treatment prevents late complications. Tick removal within 24-48 hours reduces transmission.
precautions: Wear long sleeves and tuck pants

guidance: Doxycycline or erythromycin. Watch for Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (can be severe). Prevent tick bites.
precautions: Bed net use in endemic areas

symptoms: history of rat bite or handling
guidance: Penicillin or doxycycline. Seek medical care if bitten by a rat with fever. Rat bites can also transmit other pathogens.
precautions: Seek medical care for rat bites

guidance: Doxycycline or erythromycin. Treat louse infestation. Improve hygiene. Body louse control is key.

symptoms: red or purple skin lesions (vascular proliferations)
in immunocompromised: affects liver, spleen, bone marrow
guidance: Erythromycin or doxycycline. Associated with cat scratch disease. Avoid cat scratches in immunocompromised.
Usually self-limiting. Azithromycin in severe cases. Prevent by treating flea infestations in cats, avoiding scratches.

symptoms: reddish-blue swelling on fingers or hands (rose-colored)
guidance: Penicillin or cephalexin. Wound care. Wear gloves in high-risk occupations.
precautions: Wear gloves handling fish, meat, or poultry
Seek medical care for infected injuries

symptoms: swollen painless mass with sinus tracts discharging granules (fungal balls)
guidance: Long-term antifungals (itraconazole, voriconazole) for eumycetoma; antibiotics (co-trimoxazole) for actinomycetoma. Surgery may be needed. Endemic in dry tropics.
precautions: Do not ignore chronic foot swelling
Avoid walking barefoot in endemic areas

symptoms: slow-growing warty nodules or plaques on skin (usually feet or legs)
guidance: Long-term antifungals (itraconazole, terbinafine). Surgery or cryotherapy for small lesions. Avoid trauma to skin in endemic areas.
precautions: Avoid contact with soil in endemic areas

symptoms: nodule at site of inoculation (often hand)
followed by lymphangitic spread (nodules along lymphatics)
guidance: Itraconazole for 3-6 months. Potassium iodide for severe or lymphocutaneous. Avoid contact with soil and plant matter (thorns, sphagnum moss).

symptoms: disseminated: in immunocompromised — fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, adrenal insufficiency
guidance: Amphotericin B for severe; itraconazole for mild-moderate. Avoid exposure to bird/bat droppings. Endemic in soil with high nitrogen.
precautions: Avoid disturbing bird or bat roosts
Wear masks when cleaning areas with droppings

guidance: Itraconazole for 6-12 months. Amphotericin B for severe. Avoid exposure to soil near waterways in endemic areas (North America, rare in India).
precautions: Avoid activities creating dust in endemic areas

symptoms: chronic: weight loss, fever, cough, dyspnea
guidance: Itraconazole, co-trimoxazole. Endemic in Latin America. Avoid dust exposure in endemic areas.
precautions: Avoid soil dust in endemic areas

symptoms: fever, cough, chest pain, erythema nodosum (joint pain + rash)
guidance: Fluconazole, itraconazole. Amphotericin B for severe. Avoid dust storms in endemic areas (American Southwest, rare in India).

symptoms: meningitis: headache, fever, neck stiffness, nausea, photophobia, confusion
guidance: Amphotericin B + flucytosine for meningitis, then fluconazole for maintenance. Source: soil, pigeon droppings. HIV/AIDS with CD4 < 100 should be screened.

symptoms: CHRONIC PULMONARY: cavitary lesions, weight loss, hemoptysis
INVASIVE: fever, cough, chest pain, hemoptysis (in immunocompromised)
guidance: Voriconazole is first-line for invasive. Itraconazole for allergic. Remove source of spores (construction, damp environments).

symptoms: facial pain, nasal congestion, black eschar on palate or nasal mucosa
guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — IV amphotericin B. Surgical debridement of necrotic tissue. Reverse underlying risk factors (control diabetes, stop steroids). High mortality.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is treatment of choice. Steroids for moderate-severe. Prophylaxis in HIV with CD4 < 200.
precautions: HIV patients should be on TMP-SMX prophylaxis if CD4 < 200
Seek care for persistent dry cough and dyspnea in immunocompromised

guidance: EMERGENCY — Ivermectin. Stop steroids. ICU care. Hyperinfection is often fatal. Prevent by screening at-risk patients for Strongyloides before steroid use.
precautions: Avoid unnecessary steroids in endemic areas

symptoms: then neurological: meningitis, encephalitis, myelitis, confusion, seizures, paralysis
guidance: No specific antiviral. Supportive care. Vaccination available for high-risk. Avoid tick bites.

symptoms: rash: macules → papules → vesicles → pustules → crusts
lesions can be genital or generalized
transmission: close contact, respiratory droplets, sex
guidance: Supportive care. Antivirals (tecovirimat) for severe. Isolate to prevent spread. Vaccination (JYNNEOS) for post-exposure prophylaxis (within 4 days).

symptoms: then sudden onset dyspnea, cough, hypotension (cardiogenic shock)
guidance: EMERGENCY — supportive care, oxygenation, hemodynamic support. No specific antiviral (ribavirin is controversial). Avoid contact with rodent urine/droppings.
precautions: Wear masks when cleaning rodent-contaminated areas
Do not sweep or vacuum (aerosolizes virus)

symptoms: restlessness, lethargy, sudden drop in BP
guidance: EMERGENCY — Hospitalize immediately. IV fluids, careful fluid management, platelet transfusion only if bleeding. Warning signs: abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, lethargy. Do NOT give NSAIDs. Can be fatal.
precautions: Do not take aspirin/ibuprofen — only paracetamol

symptoms: later: fatigue, jaundice, abdominal pain, nausea
guidance: Antiviral therapy (DAAs) cures >95% — available free under government schemes. Screen all baby boomers and high-risk individuals. Prevent: do not share needles, screen blood products. No vaccine.

symptoms: co-infection with Hepatitis B — can be severe
fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain, nausea
guidance: Hepatitis D only occurs with Hepatitis B. Prevention: vaccinate against Hepatitis B. Treatment: pegylated interferon (not always effective). Supportive care. Liver transplant for advanced.
precautions: Hepatitis B vaccination prevents Hepatitis D

symptoms: fever, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain
similar to Hepatitis A but more severe in pregnant women (high mortality in 3rd trimester)
guidance: Supportive care. Pregnant women with HEV need specialized care. Avoid contaminated water. Vaccine is available in China but not yet widespread in India.
precautions: Avoid raw shellfish in endemic areas
Pregnant women: be extra cautious with food and water

symptoms: not known to cause significant liver disease
co-infection with HIV may improve HIV prognosis
guidance: No treatment needed. It does not cause chronic liver disease. No vaccine.
precautions: Blood donor screening not routinely done

guidance: ORS, zinc supplementation, continued feeding. Severe dehydration: IV fluids. Rotavirus vaccine (Rotavac, RotaTeq) is part of Universal Immunization Programme in India.
ORS hydration. No antibiotics. Highly contagious — hand hygiene with soap and water (alcohol sanitizers are less effective). Isolate for 48 hours after symptoms resolve.
precautions: Avoid preparing food for others while ill

guidance: Supportive care. Good hand hygiene. No antiviral. Isolate to prevent spread. Common in children.

symptoms: painful, blistering rash in a dermatome (nerve distribution)
preceded by shooting pain or burning
post-herpetic neuralgia (chronic pain after rash heals)
guidance: Antivirals (acyclovir, valacyclovir) within 72 hours of rash. Pain management. Zoster vaccine recommended for adults over 50. Avoid contact with pregnant women and immunocompromised.
precautions: Avoid contact with varicella-susceptible persons during rash

guidance: Supportive care — rest, hydration, paracetamol. Avoid contact sports (risk of splenic rupture). No antivirals needed. Spread via saliva ('kissing disease').
precautions: Avoid sharing saliva (utensils, drinks, kissing) during active infection
Avoid strenuous activity until spleen no longer enlarged

symptoms: congenital: hearing loss, intellectual disability, microcephaly
in immunocompromised: retinitis, pneumonia, colitis, encephalitis
guidance: Immunocompetent: self-limiting. Congenital: valganciclovir. Immunocompromised: ganciclovir, foscarnet. Prevention: avoid saliva contact in immunosuppressed.
precautions: Pregnant women: avoid contact with young children's saliva
